newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Malaysia hits back over Amazon logging fears.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia hits back over Amazon logging fears.

text.p: Malaysian officials and logging companies, stung by accusations they pose a threat to the Amazon rainforest, on Wednesday accused environmentalists and Western nations of mounting a scare campaign.

Recent acquisitions of forests and sawmills by powerful logging groups from Malaysia and other Asian countries in fact represented a new source of income fo the empoverished Amazon region, they told a special committee in Brazil's Congress.

"We have been accused of devastating forests and Malaysian companies have been described as monsters coming to destroy the Amazon," Ambassador to Brazil Dat Zainal Zain said. "Please, show us one tree Malaysian companies have cut down."

He also took a swipe at what he said was a campaign by "developed Western nations who consider the Amazon region to be their backyard and feel threatend by the efficiency and advanced technology shown by Malaysian logging firms."

Environmental groups say the arrival of Asian logging companies, which operate on a larger scale than their Brazilian counterparts, will speed up deforestation in the Amazon. The congressional committee was set up this year to investigate the extent of Asian companies' involvement in the Amazon logging industry.

In a report in May, Greenpeace said the Asians devastated ecosystems in several Third World countries as they expanded to compensate for dwindling reserves at home and were moving into the Amazon, the world's largest remaining rainforest.

Zain dismissed the report as "biased and one-sided" and accused Greenpeace of "mixing up facts with half-facts and fiction." He said Malaysian firms would not follow the example of many local loggers who regularly ignore logging laws.
A recently leaked government report suggested 80 percent of logging in the Amazon was illegal, with timber coming from protected Indian reservations or national parks.
Brazilian officials say they cannot be sure exactly how many Asian logging firms have begun operations in the Amazon but have vowed they will make sure they observe local laws.

Zain confirmed the purchase last year of 742,000 acres (300,000 hectares) in a remote area of Amazonas state and of a sawmill by WTK Group, one of Malaysia's largest logging interests. Greenpeace activists recently reported they had spotted a shipment of bulldozers and tractors heading for the area bought by WTK, located between the Jurua and Purus rivers not far from Brazil's border with Peru and Bolivia.

Another deal involving Malaysian companies was announced by logging officials attending Wednesday's meeting. In April, Rimbunan Hiajau Group bought two logging firms in the city of Belem, Para state, for about $40 million, Aldebardo Klautau Filho, a lawyer representing the group, said.
